tagline: A canal tunnel, aqueduct and river falls trace an unfinished route west
intro: The Chesapeake & Ohio Canal Scenic Byway links Washington, D.C., and Cumberland over 236 miles. Maryland’s tourism office gives six to eight hours of driving and recommends three to six days for the journey. The route passes rolling farmland near Sharpsburg and crosses into West Virginia between Hancock and the Paw Paw Tunnel. Near Washington, the driving route includes River Road and the Clara Barton Parkway; the canal towpath is a separate trail for travel on foot or by bicycle.

The canal’s builders began in 1828, intending to reach the Ohio River. They reached Cumberland in 1850, eight years after the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad. Debt ended the company’s plans to continue into the Ohio Valley. Coal from the Alleghenies was its principal cargo; navigation ceased after the 1924 flood. The canal required 74 locks and eleven aqueducts to cross streams along its route.

The preserved canal and its towpath now form a national historical park. The Maryland Office of Tourism Development presents that park, its 74 lift locks and 184.5-mile towpath as the heart of the scenic byway.

Starting at Cumberland, travel through Oldtown toward Paw Paw, then cross West Virginia to Hancock. Continue by Williamsport and Sharpsburg to Brunswick, then Point of Rocks, Poolesville and Great Falls before Washington.

moments.title: Paw Paw Tunnel
moments.text: Paw Paw Tunnel cuts through 3,118 feet of mountain to bypass six miles of the Potomac’s horseshoe bends. More than six million bricks went into its construction. Work began in 1836 with completion expected within two years, but the tunnel did not open until 1850. Financial and construction problems halted work from 1841 to 1847. Even after boats began passing through, the brick lining remained unfinished. The tunnel was so narrow that people could not pass between the mules and its wall. A semaphore signal installed at the west end in 1872 controlled boat traffic.

moments.title: Williamsport
moments.text: An aqueduct, a lockhouse and a railroad lift bridge share a half-mile stretch at Williamsport. These are the Conococheague Aqueduct, Lockhouse 44 and the only railroad lift bridge on the canal. Rail and water transportation worked together here: in 1873, the Western Maryland Railway extended its line from Hagerstown to reach canal traffic. Coal from Cumberland-area mines moved from barges into rail cars at Williamsport. A flood badly damaged the canal in 1924, ending its commercial operation. The canal visitor center is at Cushwa Basin. The town’s historic core became a National Register historic district in 2001.
moments.notice: The Conococheague Aqueduct, Lockhouse 44 and railroad lift bridge fit within a half-mile stretch.

moments.title: Great Falls
moments.text: At Great Falls, the Potomac drops 76 feet in less than a mile. The river narrows through the falls and Mather Gorge. Canal builders tried two sides of this obstacle. On the Virginia bank, the eighteenth-century Patowmack Canal used five locks to let barges avoid the falls. The later C&O Canal followed the Maryland side, ultimately linking Cumberland with the Potomac tidewater. Great Falls Tavern now houses a visitor center, and the trail on Olmsted Island offers views of the falls. The C&O also drew water from the falls through a feeder that is now abandoned.
moments.notice: The Potomac narrows as it passes over the falls and through Mather Gorge.
